Just who he may be is mysterious; but whoever he be, let him tremble at the sound of furious hoofs and rustling silken robes.

Mrs. Elizabeth Tyler is very clear on the silken robes part. The masks are silken, too, though whether the tar, feathers and rods are carried in vanity cases or in those stunning new peacock feather wrist bags, she did not say. Mrs. Tyler is the leading lady of the Ku Klux Klan. She arrived in this city right after the officials had rebuffed some men Ku Kluxers who were caught forming a chapter here.

Rebuffs here fail to dishearten Mrs. Tyler. No sooner had she arrived from Atlanta than she announced that 100 letters of inquiry had reached her in two days. "95 per cent of them from women." Indeed, it appears that New York women are looking to join the Klan. Before long the shops ought to blossom with pearl handled whips jewel studded and daintily suited to a lady's grasp.

Masculine Kluxers have to get along with cotton robes. But Southern gallantry to the sex has dictated silken robes for lady night riders. And this silken costume, as Mrs. Tyler prettily points out, is not half so dreadful as has been pictured.

Can Rock Many Things

Women, it must be admitted, are beginning to realize that the hand which rocks the cradle can rock quite a number of things when it gets going. It rocked the ballot box this week, for instance, and the town saw all the primary candidates for mayor wheedling and lauding the republican women who, as it appeared, held the balance of power. The fact that they threw the balance in Curran's favor is a tribute to their domesticity, for on the eve of the primary Mr. Curran told the republican women that municipal government is just like house cleaning. As a matter of fact if running a city were half so hard as house cleaning, women would long ago have been handed the job.

Meanwhile, the Smiths can't speak to the Auerbachs. Why they should want to speak to each other after the things they've said about each other is question. But even if they think up brand new impertinencies, they are barred by the court from hollering them across the vestibule at 24 Riverside Drive, or up the speaking tube. Mrs. J. Bradley Smith complained about what Mrs. Louis Auerbach said, and Mrs. Auerbach told the magistrate what Mrs. Smith said, and after soothing both of them with a remark about "ladies of culture and refinement" the magistrate made them promise never again to interfere or communicate with each other. If it had happened anywhere except in a fashionable apartment house the quarrel would have smoothed itself out without official interposition.

Such Is City Life

But that's what comes of living in a city. You can't even put itching powder down boys' backs for a joke without being sent up for a couple of weeks. A man found that out, to his sorrow, the other day.

An entirely new method of weight reducing has been discovered by Miss Milla Gade, the Danish swimming champion. Miss Gade, who recently swam around Manhattan Island, has completed a swim from Albany to New York. She finds that by swimming 163 miles in something over 6 hours (the hours distributed however over six days) at an average speed of two miles an hour, one can talk off six pounds. Anyone is welcome to the recipe.

Ellis Island officials are also losing weight daily in their efforts to make Steffina tell where she comes from. Carolina. The 22-year-old arrived at the Island after the month's quota of immigrants from Poland had been admitted. Hence Carolina was booked for deportation. But Steffina, who has spent most of her 22 years in this country, thought differently. So on visiting day, Steffina changed clothes with Carolina and Carolina slipped away to parts unknown. Steffina, threatened with deportation in Carolina's place, has gone on hunger strike so effectually that she is too weak to be deported. The officials are at their wits' ends.

Meanwhile, Tale Sedlin thought he'd have to go back to Moscow because rents were too high in New York for a shoe lace vender. But he stumbled into a roofless cellar in the Bronx. The other day he confessed that for years he has lived in this hole, unroofed except for a few planks on rainy nights, and now he is such a fresh air enthusiast that he would not dwell in a steam heated flat if you paid the rent for him.

His Own Coin

Sedlin, for example escapes a dispute with landlord such as Mrs. Nancy Stenecke has. The landlord accused her of robbing his cash box in order to pay her rent, which after all looks like a case of paying him in his own coin.

The rise in the rate of burglaries is what worries Mayor Fly.
